module8: Capstone: build, review and teach a small solution
Now you put everything together and help others learn it.
Plan a small solution: data model, rules, a flow, one class and one screen.
Run a peer code review using a short checklist.
Write a one-page guide so a new developer can maintain your work.
Teach one part of it in a ten-minute session.
A learner builds a case-tracking app, a peer finds a query inside a loop, the learner fixes it, and a new colleague then extends the app using the guide alone.
Build a small solution for a service business, review a peer's work, and teach one part of it.
Show that the solution works, passes tests and has a guide, and that a peer can extend it without help.
quiz: A custom object called Job must belong to an Account. Which relationship would you use and why?
A lookup or master-detail relationship from Job to Account. Master-detail fits if a job should never exist without its account and should be deleted with it; a lookup is looser.
Write the idea of a validation rule that stops a close date in the past. When does it fire?
It checks that close date is not earlier than today and shows an error message. It fires when a user tries to save the record, so bad data never gets stored.
Why are formulas and validation rules tried before code?
They are easier to build, easier to read for admins, and need no tests or deployment effort. Code is used only when they cannot do the job.
A record-triggered flow sends an email but the email address is blank. What should you have built?
A fault path that catches the error and sends a clear message to an admin or logs it. Without it the flow fails silently or shows users a confusing error.
A trigger runs a query inside a loop over 200 records. What is the problem and the fix?
It makes 200 queries and will hit the platform limit on queries. Collect the IDs first, run one query outside the loop, and use a map to look up results.
Why keep logic in a class and only a thin trigger on each object?
The class can be tested and reused, and one trigger per object avoids unclear run order. The trigger just passes records to the class.
Name two things that make a screen component accessible.
Clear labels and good colour contrast, and use by keyboard alone. Also useful: text alternatives for images and a sensible reading order.
An outside order system calls your CRM and sometimes times out. How do you design for it?
Use a retry with waiting time between tries, log every failure, and make the call safe to repeat so an order is not created twice. Keep credentials in a secure store, not in code.
A release has 70% test coverage and the platform needs 75%. What do you do and what else goes in the release note?
Write more meaningful tests until coverage passes, rather than skipping the rule. The note should also list the changes and a rollback step.
In your capstone, a peer review finds a hard-coded secret in a class. What is the action and why?
Move it to a secure credential store and change the secret, because anyone who can read the code can see it. Then add the check to the review list.
ladder: L1 Basic: Know the words
Remember the basic terms: object, field, record, relationship and flow. Name what each one is for in simple words.
Say each term once and show it on screen. Check the learner can point to a field and a record. Common mistake: mixing up an object with a record.
L2 Awareness: See the big picture
Understand how data, rules, automation and screens fit together in a CRM. Explain why low-code is tried before code.
Draw one picture of the layers. Ask the learner to explain it back in their own words. Common mistake: thinking code is always better.
L3 Foundation: Build simple things
Apply what you know to build objects, fields, formulas and a simple validation rule. Test them with good and bad data.
Give a small case and watch them build it. Check names follow the standard. Common mistake: testing only with good data.
L4 Practitioner: Automate and code safely
Apply flows with fault paths and write a bulk-safe trigger with a class. Analyse a failing flow and find the cause.
Provide a broken flow and a trigger with a query in a loop. Check they fix both. Common mistake: ignoring limits until the live system fails.
L5 Specialist: Connect and test
Analyse an integration and evaluate its failure plan. Write tests that prove the work and prepare a release with rollback.
Ask for the retry and logging plan before the code. Check coverage and rollback note. Common mistake: secrets saved in code.
L6 Advanced: Design and review
Evaluate other people's designs and code against a checklist. Create a design that balances low-code, code and cost.
Run a peer review with the checklist. Check feedback is specific and kind. Common mistake: reviewing style only and missing risk.
L7 Super expert: Lead and teach
Create a whole solution, set the standards for a team and teach others to follow them. Evaluate trade-offs across the full platform.
Ask the learner to teach one topic and review a team's design. Check the guide lets a newcomer continue alone. Common mistake: keeping knowledge in one head.
